intro: You grow up in a close, church-centred family in segregated Atlanta, and you learn to speak to a crowd. Your tools are words, organising and a movement of thousands; your opponents are laws, threats and an FBI that watches you.

office.why: Law: segregation laws decided where he could sit, eat and learn.

rope.why: Safety: a bomb at home, a stabbing, jail and FBI surveillance.

bridge.why: Church and family: a community that carried the movement.

ladder.why: Education: Morehouse at 15 and a doctorate opened a path for his voice.

advantage.title: Staying power
advantage.text: The movement held after bombings, arrests and setbacks. A wrong step does not send you back: others pick up the work and you stay in place.

life.title: Atlanta, 1929
life.text: Born on 15 January 1929 as Michael King Jr. into a family of pastors; his father later changes both their names to Martin. The home is comfortable, but outside it segregation laws shape every part of life.

life.title: “You can’t play with us”
life.text: As a small child, Martin is told his white friend can no longer play with him. His parents explain that racism exists, and that he must never think he is “less”.

life.title: The bus ride home
life.text: At 14, after winning a speech contest, Martin rides home by bus. The driver orders him and his teacher to give up their seats to white passengers, and they stand for about 90 miles. He later calls it the angriest night of his life.

life.title: College at 15
life.text: Martin enters Morehouse College at 15. His teachers show him that faith and the fight for justice belong together.

life.title: Learning from Gandhi
life.text: In seminary and graduate school, Martin studies how others have resisted injustice. One leader from India shapes his ideas of peaceful protest.

q.q: Whose nonviolent resistance inspired King’s approach?
q.x: Gandhi led nonviolent campaigns against British rule in India. King adapted these ideas for the American civil rights movement.

life.title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
life.text: In December 1955 the 26-year-old pastor is chosen to lead the Montgomery Improvement Association. For 381 days thousands of people refuse the buses, and the segregation law falls.

life.title: Bomb at the front door
life.text: On 30 January 1956 a bomb explodes at the King home while Coretta and their baby are inside. No one is hurt. Martin asks the angry crowd outside not to answer violence with violence.

life.title: Jail in Birmingham
life.text: In April 1963 Martin is arrested during protests against segregation in Birmingham, Alabama. From his cell he writes a letter explaining why waiting for justice is not an option.

life.title: “I Have a Dream”
life.text: On 28 August 1963 about 250,000 people gather in Washington for jobs and freedom. Martin gives his famous speech at the Lincoln Memorial, one voice among many organisers and speakers.

life.title: Laws change
life.text: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 bans segregation in public places and discrimination at work. After the marches in Selma, another law follows. At 35 Martin receives the Nobel Peace Prize.

q.q: Which 1965 law protected the right to vote?
q.x: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 followed the Selma marches and targeted barriers like literacy tests that kept Black citizens from voting.

life.title: A harder fight
life.text: Martin speaks out against the Vietnam War and for poor people of every race. Many allies and politicians turn away, and the FBI watches him and tries to damage his name.

life.title: Memphis, 1968 and after
life.text: Martin goes to Memphis to support striking sanitation workers. On 4 April 1968 he is assassinated, aged 39. Since 1986 the US marks Martin Luther King Jr. Day, and the movement’s laws still protect millions.

sources: Nobel Prize: Martin Luther King Jr. biography
flags: Ages and dates follow the single-player tiles; 90-mile bus ride and 'angriest night' wording from King's own recollection as cited there.

evidence.ev: Segregation laws shaped his childhood in Atlanta; on a bus ride at 15 he was made to stand for about 90 miles.
His house was bombed in 1956, he was stabbed in 1958, jailed in Birmingham in 1963 and watched by the FBI.
His family and the Ebenezer Baptist Church were a strong base for him.
He entered Morehouse College at 15 and earned a doctorate at Boston University in 1955.
